Invest a lump sum now or in stages? Keep the waiting cash in the picture

Four charts compare equal starting capital, a fixed buying schedule and invented market shocks, with every dollar of waiting cash included in the result.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare equal starting capital over one invented market year

Interactive planning lab

Month-12 total with immediate investment$50,880
Month-12 total with staged investment$58,983.89
Staged minus immediate at month 12$8,103.89

One invented 12-month market path, no historical returns or assigned probabilities. All capital exists before month one. Immediate investment deploys all of it before the first return; staged investment makes equal transfers of starting principal at the beginning of each selected month, starting immediately. Uninvested cash earns the effective annual cash rate converted monthly, and that interest remains in cash. The selected market trend is an effective annual rate converted monthly. The one-off shock multiplies that month’s market factor; it is not added to the annual return. Fractional units and costless transfers are assumed. All paths retain waiting cash and its interest in total wealth. No dividends, tax, fees, slippage, account limits or inflation are modeled. A fixed purchase schedule is not a capital guarantee.

The central idea

Staging changes when capital takes market risk. Its result depends on the path, the waiting-cash return and the schedule; it does not guarantee a better purchase price.

01

Start with the same money available at the same date

A lump-sum decision begins with capital already in hand. That is different from investing part of each future paycheque: future earnings are not available for an immediate investment today. This comparison gives both schedules the entire starting amount before the first month.

The immediate schedule invests all the capital at once. The staged schedule divides the starting principal into equal purchases at the beginnings of the selected months, with the first purchase made immediately. Both strategies then experience the same invented market path and finish after twelve months.

Investor.gov describes dollar-cost averaging as regular equal-dollar purchases regardless of market fluctuations. That definition establishes a process, not a promise about the result of delaying an existing lump sum. These charts investigate the mechanics of one schedule and do not estimate the historical frequency with which either strategy has won.

02

Separate the market path from the investment schedule

The first chart shows a synthetic market index starting at 100. Every month has the same underlying trend factor, except for one month that also receives the selected shock. Both factors multiply. A negative 20% shock is a 0.80 multiplier; it is not a subtraction of twenty percentage points from the annual trend.

The final index is 100 × (1 + annual trend) × (1 + shock), using the percentage inputs as decimal rates. Moving the shock from month two to month twelve preserves that endpoint. It changes which staged purchases have already been exposed when the shock arrives.

This is a controlled thought experiment. It contains one hand-selected shock and a smooth background trend, with no other volatility. It is neither a realistic simulation of a full market cycle nor a forecast of the next year. A negative shock can occur after all the staged capital has been invested; a positive shock can also reward the money that was deployed earlier.

03

Include the investment account and the waiting account

The second chart compares total wealth: invested assets plus cash and cash interest. Looking only at the investment account would make the staged strategy appear artificially small while some of its original principal is still waiting. The cash-only line provides another reference using the same starting capital.

In the original worked example, CAD 60,000 is invested immediately or in six equal purchases. The market trend is 6%, with an additional negative 20% shock in month two; waiting cash earns an assumed effective 3% annually. At month twelve the immediate case is CAD 50,880, while the staged case is approximately CAD 58,984 including its retained cash interest.

Those are original calculations for these specific inputs. They demonstrate an early-loss path in which some staged capital enters later. They do not establish a general advantage. Set the shock to zero and the comparison becomes a different question: how much exposure to the underlying trend is forgone while cash waits?

04

The timing matrix explains why the answer can change

The third chart separates invested asset value from waiting cash at selected dates. Month zero follows the first purchase and precedes the first return. The original principal is completely transferred by the last scheduled purchase; cash interest stays in the waiting account rather than being added to later instalments.

The fourth chart replaces the shock size and month while preserving the chosen starting capital, staging duration, cash rate and underlying trend. It reports staged wealth minus immediate wealth at the common finish. A positive number favours staging in that cell; a negative number favours immediate investment.

Read across a row to isolate order. Immediate investment ends with the same amount across that row because all capital experiences the same twelve multipliers. Staged investment can change because different purchases experience different subsets. Once all principal has entered the market, moving a later shock among those fully invested months leaves its endpoint unchanged, apart from rounding.

05

Choose a process that fits the goal and can survive a different path

Before selecting a buying schedule, separate money needed for near-term bills and decide how much market risk the long-term goal can bear. A timetable for buying a risky asset does not make that asset suitable for a fixed near-term payment. Staging can still produce a loss after the final purchase.

Write down the amount and dates in advance, the treatment of waiting cash, and what would justify changing the plan. A process that depends on buying only after a fall needs a separate decision rule and may leave cash waiting indefinitely. This tool uses a predetermined schedule rather than such a timing rule.

Real implementation also involves fund expenses, transaction costs, taxes, spreads and account restrictions. Cash yields can change, and investment returns do not follow a smooth trend. Use the graphics to understand exposure and timing, then test additional paths. No cell is assigned a probability, and the tool does not recommend a security, an allocation or a preferred date.
